title: Reusable Django Applications
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of reusable django applications and at least two listed subtopics.

content.intro: Learn reusable django applications through a compact visual, an inspectable Django example, and a practical verification task.
content.why_it_matters: Reusable Django Applications matters because a Django project has to behave predictably across requests, database state, configuration, and deployments. Understanding this piece makes the surrounding application easier to test, maintain, and secure.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: This lesson examines reusable django applications as part of advanced django architecture. The objective is to understand the behavior, connect it to the listed subtopics, and verify it with a small example rather than relying on memorized syntax.

content_blocks.title: What to cover
content_blocks.text: The source syllabus for this lesson names: Reusable-app structure; Package metadata; App configuration; Migrations and templates; Versioning and dependency compatibility. Keep these distinct concepts together: know what each item does, when it applies, and what assumption must be verified in your project.

items.title: Reusable-app structure
items.text: For Reusable-app structure, identify the Django component responsible, the inputs and outputs it owns, and the boundary conditions that matter. Use the accompanying example as a starting point, verify it with the official versioned documentation, and record one test demonstrating expected behavior.

items.title: Package metadata
items.text: Package metadata affects persistence and data correctness. Keep invariants in validation and database constraints where appropriate, inspect generated SQL/migrations, and test both expected data and error/rollback behavior.

items.title: App configuration
items.text: Configuration for App configuration should be explicit, environment-aware, and validated before serving requests. Record defaults and deploy-specific values, keep secrets outside committed content, and test the setting that changes behavior.

items.title: Migrations and templates
items.text: A migration is a versioned, ordered schema/data operation. `makemigrations` creates files; `migrate` applies them. Review generated operations and test the forward path and recovery plan using representative data.

items.title: Versioning and dependency compatibility
items.text: For Versioning and dependency compatibility, identify the Django component responsible, the inputs and outputs it owns, and the boundary conditions that matter. Use the accompanying example as a starting point, verify it with the official versioned documentation, and record one test demonstrating expected behavior.

content_blocks.title: Worked example: Reusable Django Applications
content_blocks.code:
python manage.py showmigrations
python manage.py makemigrations --check
python manage.py migrate --plan
content_blocks.expected_output: These commands inspect migration state, check for model changes without migration files, and show a plan to apply migrations.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Open a local project using the documented Django 6.1-compatible Python environment. If this snippet depends on model names, URL configuration, settings, or an optional package, add those prerequisites before running it. Otherwise inspect it as a static example. CodeLeaf browser preview does not execute Django/Python server code.
content_blocks.troubleshooting: Do not delete or rewrite migration history as a quick fix. Review dependency graphs, backup and test the proposed migration on a safe database.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Change one input or configuration choice related to Reusable-app structure. Write down the expected outcome, test one normal case and one invalid or boundary case, then record what changed. Do not add real credentials or sensitive production data.

content_blocks.title: Common mistakes and fixes
content_blocks.text: Common pitfalls include skipping a required configuration/import, copying a fragment without its model or URL context, trusting client input, or treating a development-only behavior as production-ready. Check the earliest failing assumption, consult the version-specific docs, and add a regression test for the failure you found.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a framework fragment without its imports, configuration, model, or URL context.
common_mistakes.why: The snippet may be incomplete when separated from a Django project.
common_mistakes.fix: Use the stated prerequisites and run the relevant management check or focused test.

common_mistakes.problem: Trusting input or relying only on a happy-path example.
common_mistakes.why: Invalid values, unauthorized requests, or concurrent activity can violate assumptions.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and add a negative or boundary test.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating the development sample as production-ready.
common_mistakes.why: Production hosting, secrets, storage, monitoring and resource limits differ from local use.
common_mistakes.fix: Follow the current deployment/security references and document untested areas.
